title: How do we take two thirds away from three fourths?
description: Three fourths and two thirds count pieces of different sizes, so both are changed to twelfths. Then the twelfths are taken away. Keeko's doubt is that the top numbers and the bottom numbers can both be taken away.
teaching_notes: One idea: fractions with different bottom numbers are first changed to equal fractions with a common bottom number, and then the top numbers are taken away. Watch for students who take away the tops and the bottoms separately.

video_script.why: The child sees that fractions with different fractional units must first be written with one common denominator before the top numbers are taken away.
video_script.substitution: The book's solved question of three fourths take away two thirds, solved with the common denominator twelve.
video_script.anchor: a strip cut into fourths and a strip cut into thirds, both then redrawn as twelfths
video_script.wrong_answer: take away the tops and take away the bottoms
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes away the tops and the bottoms, so three fourths take away two thirds becomes one over one, a whole, which is more than the three fourths we began with.
video_script.payoff_line: Three fourths take away two thirds leaves one twelfth
video_script.fraction_reading: three fourths, two thirds, nine twelfths, eight twelfths, one twelfth
never_show: the answer 1/12 before the answer beat
maths_rules: 1 and 12 have no common factor other than 1, so 1/12 is in lowest terms
Keeko's slip: (3 − 2)/(4 − 3) = 1/1 = 1, which is more than 3/4
video_script.design: Two strips with different cuts are redrawn as twelfths. The take away happens only after both strips have the same fractional unit.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a strip cut into 4 equal parts with 3 shaded, and a strip cut into 3 equal parts with 2 shaded; the words 3/4 − 2/3

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.two: the two strips appear, 3/4 and 2/3 shaded
marks.ask: the two kinds of part glow in turn to show their different sizes

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about taking away fractions.
<bookmark mark='two'/>We want three fourths take away two thirds.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The pieces are fourths and thirds, which are different sizes. What could we do to make them the same size?

beats.on_screen: the two strips hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the fourths strip and the thirds strip side by side; both are cut again into 12 equal parts; the label common denominator appears

marks.units: the fourths and the thirds glow to show different sizes
marks.common: both strips are cut into 12 equal parts and the label common denominator appears
marks.equal: the new shaded parts cover the same length as the old ones

narration: <bookmark mark='units'/>Three fourths counts fourths, and two thirds counts thirds. We cannot take away pieces of different sizes.
<bookmark mark='common'/>We change both to a bottom number that both can share. This bottom number is called a common denominator.
<bookmark mark='equal'/>The new fractions are equal in size to the old ones. Fractions equal in size are called equivalent fractions.

beats.on_screen: Given: 3/4 and 2/3, with different bottom numbers 4 and 3

marks.given: the two fractions are written on the working board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three fourths and two thirds, which have different bottom numbers.

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find three fourths take away two thirds.

marks.common: 4 × 3 = 12 is written and the number 12 glows

narration: <bookmark mark='common'/>Step one, find a common denominator, because both four and three go into twelve.
We multiply the two bottom numbers. Four times three is twelve.

marks.mult: the top 3 and the bottom 4 are each multiplied by 3

narration: <bookmark mark='mult'/>Step two, change three fourths into twelfths. Multiply the top and the bottom by three, because four times three is twelve.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>Three times three is nine, and four times three is twelve.

marks.mult: the top 2 and the bottom 3 are each multiplied by 4

narration: <bookmark mark='mult'/>Step three, change two thirds into twelfths. Multiply the top and the bottom by four, because three times four is twelve.
<bookmark mark='eight'/>Two times four is eight, and three times four is twelve.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: 9/12 − 8/12 = (9 − 8)/12; 9 − 8 = 1 part of the twelfth unit

marks.same: the two fractions 9/12 and 8/12 line up with the same bottom number
marks.take: 8 parts slide off the 9 shaded parts and 1 part stays

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step four, take away the tops and keep the bottom, because both fractions now count twelfths.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Nine take away eight leaves one part.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 3/4 − 2/3 = 1/12 of the whole; 1 and 12 share no factor but 1

marks.low: a note says it cannot be made smaller

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Three fourths take away two thirds leaves one twelfth.
<bookmark mark='low'/>It cannot be made smaller, because one and twelve share no factor except one.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the strips
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 3 − 2 = 1 on top and 4 − 3 = 1 at the bottom, giving 1 over 1 = one whole; a full strip appears beside the 3/4 strip and is longer; the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows the tops and the bottoms both taken away
marks.whole: a full strip appears and is longer than the three fourths strip
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and the strips are cut into twelfths

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we take away the tops and take away the bottoms.
Three take away two leaves one, and four take away three leaves one.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>That gives one over one, which is one whole.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But we began with only three fourths, and taking away cannot leave more than we began with.
Fourths and thirds must first become twelfths.
